text: Elements: A River Worth Returning To
Starting from four storybook elements, travel from an orchard to a coastal gathering. Make useful things for people you meet. The world remembers what you leave behind.
Earth
Loose ground containing mineral grains and clay. Plants can grow in suitable soil.
Water
A liquid that flows, soaks materials and takes the shape of its container.
Air
The gases around us. Moving air can carry moisture, fill a sail and supply oxygen to a flame.
Fire
Burning produces heat and light. Heat can cook food and change materials.
Clay
Soft, fine earth that holds an impressed shape while wet.
Stone
Hard, rough mineral material; its weight and abrasive surfaces can do work.
Formed clay bowl
A shaped, dried clay bowl that has not been fired. It can serve as a dry form, but is not ready to hold water.
Brick
A hard, regular block of fired clay, made for stacking into lasting structures.
Rain
Water arriving from the sky, enough to soak the ground rather than fill a vessel neatly.
Plant
A living stem with roots and leaves; a source of several different natural materials.
Grain
Dry edible seeds with a tough outer surface and a starchy interior.
Flour
Fine meal ground from grain. Loose and powdery until it is wetted.
Dough
A soft mass of flour and water. It can hold its shape, but has not yet risen or baked.
Flatbread
A simple cooked bread without a raised, airy crumb.
Fruit
Ripe, juicy produce with flesh around its seeds.
Fruit juice
The fruit's liquid, separated from its flesh; sweet enough to feed fermentation.
Sand
Small, hard mineral grains. Loose when poured, abrasive when rubbed.
Glass
A hard, clear material that lets light through but needs shaping to give it a particular job.
Wood
Rough timber: solid lengths with grain and bulk, not flat boards yet.
Window
A pane held in a wooden frame, admitting light while closing an opening.
Plant fiber
Flexible strands taken from plants. They can be spun into thread or made into sheets.
Thread
A long, fine strand spun from fibers; useful for binding and stitching.
Cloth
A flexible sheet made from interlaced threads.
Rope
Thick cord made to hold loads or tie larger pieces together.
Sleeping mat
A padded woven surface that separates a sleeper from the cold ground.
House
A small weatherproof home with solid walls and a timber roof. A window admits daylight; a sleeping mat makes a place to rest. A stone hearth can warm the room.
Axe
A sharp stone edge on a handle. Its job is to cut and shape wood, not to pound it.
Planks
Flat, cut boards with broad faces and straight edges; easier to join into surfaces than rough timber.
Footbridge
A narrow deck spanning the brook, supported and held together above the water.
Wheel
A solid wooden disc, shaped to roll or turn around its centre. Its rim is still smooth.
Wheelset
Wheels mounted on an axle. They can roll, but still need a body to carry a load.
Handcart
A small rolling platform for moving a load by hand.
Waterwheel
A paddled wheel that moving water can turn. Its turning force still needs a connection to useful work.
Millstone
A heavy circular grinding stone. It can crush grain, but will not turn by itself.
Wooden gear
A wooden wheel with teeth that transfer turning motion to another part.
Mill gearing
A connected drive taking rotation from the waterwheel toward the grinding machinery.
Grain mill
A water-driven grinding machine built for the village's daily grain, not just a single handful.
Sack
A stitched cloth bag, closed at the sides and open at the top.
Flour sack
A sack filled with flour, ready to take to the baker.
Wild starter
A culture of microorganisms in flour and water. Given time, it produces gas that helps dough rise.
Risen dough
Dough expanded by gas from fermentation, with bubbles held inside it.
Bread
A baked loaf with an airy crumb and a firm crust.
Basket
A woven plant-fiber carrier with a rope-bound rim and handle.
Picnic basket
A basket packed with bread for a journey.
Jam
Fruit cooked down into a thick spread; it still needs a vessel for keeping.
Clay jar
A hollow clay container with a broad mouth, shaped using the bowl as a form.
Jar lid
A fitted wooden cover for the mouth of a jar.
Preserve jar
A jar filled with fruit preserve, but not yet covered.
Sealed preserves
Fruit preserve put away in a covered jar for later meals.
Cider
Fruit juice changed by fermentation into an alcoholic drink.
Glaze
A coating that forms a smooth, glass-like surface when pottery is fired.
Glazed clay jar
The same clay jar after coating and firing, with a smooth glassy surface. Its broad mouth and ceramic body remain unchanged.
Cider jar
The glazed clay jar filled with cider and closed for carrying.
Kiln
An enclosed firing chamber that concentrates heat around pottery or other materials.
Tile
A flat, regular piece of shaped clay for covering a surface.
Fired glazed bowl
A fired bowl with a smooth, finished surface rather than bare porous clay.
Table
A sturdy raised wooden surface for preparing, displaying or serving things.
Tiled table
A table with a durable tiled top, easy to wipe after a shared meal.
Stone hammer
A hard, rounded stone held in the hand for breaking and pounding; it has no handle.
Iron ore
Rock containing iron-bearing minerals, not usable metal yet.
Bellows
A flexible air chamber that pushes a directed flow into a fire.
Forge
A metalworker's hot hearth, with bellows to supply air and tools for shaping the metal.
Iron
A metal that can be shaped into tools, fasteners and fittings.
Pickaxe
A pointed metal head on a handle, suited to breaking hard ground and rock.
Carving tool
A sharpened metal cutting tool for careful shaping rather than broad chopping.
Nails
Pointed metal fasteners; their stems can also serve as small pins.
Hinge
A joint that lets a door or lid swing while staying attached.
Wooden chest
A box assembled from boards, with room to protect things inside.
Raft
Timbers bound into a floating platform, without a sail.
Sail
A broad sheet rigged to catch the wind and pull on its lines.
Sailboat
A small floating craft able to use the wind for movement.
Pier post
A stout prepared post, ready to support a landing above the water.
Dock
A fixed landing where a boat can meet the shore.
Charcoal
A carbon-rich fuel made by heating wood with limited air.
Oil-wick torch
An oil-soaked fiber head secured to a wooden support; a small portable flame, not loose charcoal balanced on timber.
Lantern
A light protected by a clear enclosure rather than left as an exposed flame.
Tower
A tall masonry structure with an opening to look out from above its surroundings.
Lighthouse
A high harbour light that can be seen from the water.
Float
A buoyant, sealed object that stays on the water's surface.
Mooring buoy
A floating marker with a line to hold a boat in place.
Oil-bearing seeds
Oil-bearing seeds selected from the mature garden harvest; some are kept for planting and some can be pressed.
Seedlings
Young growing plants, still tender and in need of support or shelter.
Trellis
An open framework of stretched lines, giving climbing stems something to grip.
Climbing garden
Young plants trained up a trellis rather than left to trail on the ground.
Greenhouse
A light-filled shelter protecting tender plants from the weather.
Saw
A toothed metal edge for cutting wood along a controlled line.
Hollow pipe
A wooden pipe with a passage through its length for water.
Reservoir
A clay-lined brick storage basin set above the growing beds, ready to receive water lifted from the stream.
Filled reservoir
A raised storage basin supplied by the waterwheel’s scooping jars rather than carried buckets.
Water channel
A supported waterway directing flow along a planned route.
Irrigation channel
A channel connected to the stored water supply.
Irrigated garden
The climbing garden with water delivered to its beds.
Flowers
The colourful blossoms of a living plant.
Dye
Colour extracted into a liquid, able to stain absorbent material.
Dyed cloth
Cloth that has taken up colour through its fibers.
Loom
A frame that holds threads under tension so they can be woven in order.
Patterned cloth
Woven cloth with a deliberate arrangement of colours.
Festival banner
A patterned flag on a support, visible above the crowd.
Awning
Cloth stretched over a supporting frame to give shade.
Canopy
A supported and tied covering sheltering a larger open space.
Paper pulp
Wet, separated plant fibers suspended in water.
Paper
A thin, dry sheet of joined fibers; a surface for marks and records.
Ink
Dark liquid pigment that leaves a readable mark on a light surface.
Printing block
A wooden face carved with a design that can be repeated.
Inked printing block
A printing face coated with ink on its raised surfaces.
Printed invitations
Printed invitations to music and a shared meal in the village square.
Letter
A written message that can travel separately from its author.
Mailboat
A boat carrying written messages between settlements.
Hollow tube
A small wooden tube with an open interior, ready to carry air or hold aligned parts.
Flute
A hollow wind instrument whose vibrating air makes a note.
Drum
A stretched surface over a hollow body, resonating when struck.
Platform
A flat, supported deck raised above the ground.
Bandstand
A sheltered raised place where musicians can gather and be heard.
Puppet
A small figure made to be moved while telling a story.
Curtain
Hanging cloth that can cover or reveal an opening.
Stage
A raised performance space with a curtain to reveal the action.
Puppet theatre
A little performance stage built around moving figures and their stories.
Paint
A coloured material spread onto a surface to make an image or coating.
Brush
Flexible fibers gathered at the end of a small handle for applying colour.
Picture
A deliberately painted image, not merely a blank sheet or a pot of colour.
Bound book
A stack of pages held together along one edge, ready to preserve a sequence.
Picture book
A bound sequence of images that can tell a story after the storyteller leaves.
Lens
A shaped, polished piece of glass that bends light.
Magnifier
A lens held in a frame for examining nearby small details.
Telescope
Lenses aligned in a tube for viewing things that are far away.
Microscope
Magnifying optics arranged to look through a thin sample. A prepared pond slide can finally show what the collected drop contains.
Glass slide
A small, flat, clear glass support, prepared on a wooden backing board; it holds a thin sample for the microscope.
Pond water
A drop collected from the pond. It may contain living things too small to see unaided.
Pond slide
A thin sample of pond water on clear glass, ready to examine through the microscope.
Pressed plant specimen
A flattened, preserved plant sample retaining its visible form.
Herbarium
A bound collection of preserved plant specimens with room for their records.
Leaf study
An observed account of a leaf's small structures, seen through a lens.
Botanical drawing
A recorded plant study showing the features an observer noticed.
Illustrated flora
A guide joining preserved specimens to drawings of their distinguishing features.
Clear collector with level marks

The marks let you compare water levels in this same vessel after equal periods of rain. Empty it between observations. Its shape means the marks are not millimetres of rainfall or equal amounts of water.
Collected rain level
Rain collected in the clear marked bottle, ready to compare with another equal-duration collection in the same vessel.
Windsock
A light fabric tube that turns and extends with the wind.
Rain record
A record comparing water levels collected in the same vessel over equal periods of rain.
Weather record
An account bringing relative collected-rain levels and wind observations together.
Net
An open mesh that can let water through while catching larger things.
Fish
A catch brought from the shore, still in need of preparation for keeping.
Brine
Salt-rich water collected from the tidal pools.
Salt
The mineral left after salty water evaporates.
Smoke
The airborne products of a smouldering wood fire, not the heat alone.
Smoked fish
Fish treated with smoke for the journey. Smoking alone does not guarantee that fish is safe to store.
Vinegar
A sharp, acidic liquid made as a fermented drink changes in contact with air.
Pickles
Fruit preserved in an acidic liquid rather than eaten fresh.
Pickle jar
A container holding the prepared pickles for transport.
Filter bed
Layers of granular material that can catch some suspended matter from water.
Water filter
A filter bed held in a conduit so water can pass through it.
Filtered water
Water after passing through the filter; clearer does not automatically mean safe.
Boiled water
Water that has been heated to boiling; this is not a promise to remove every contaminant.
Drinking-water bowl
A serving bowl filled with the prepared water for our visitors.
Covered clay jar
The glazed clay jar fitted with a removable wooden lid. It is still empty.
Covered water jar
The same clay serving jar, filled with prepared water and covered with its removable lid.
Washstand
A basin held at a comfortable height for washing.
Grain bin
A substantial wooden store for dry grain.
Drying rack
An open frame and mesh allowing air to reach food from several sides.
Dried fruit
Fruit from which much of the moisture has been removed.
Crock
A thick-walled clay storage vessel, sturdier than the small jar.
Lidded crock
A storage crock fitted with its cover.
Fruit crock
A covered crock holding dried fruit for later meals.
Seed oil
Oil pressed from seeds. A wick can draw it up to feed a flame.
Oil-soaked fiber wick
Absorbent plant fibres soaked with oil to supply a small flame.
Oil lamp
A small vessel holding oil and a wick for a steady light.
Watch lamp
An oil light protected by glass for the night watch.
Paper lantern frame
A light wooden framework covered in paper, awaiting its source of light.
Paper lantern
A small light enclosed in a paper-covered frame.
Floating lantern
A lantern supported upright on a buoyant base.
Hourglass
Two clear glass bulbs joined by a narrow passage let a measured amount of sand fall from one chamber to the other.
Pendulum
A suspended weight that swings back and forth with a regular rhythm.
Clockwork
Powered moving parts whose motion is regulated for keeping time.
Clock
A housed timekeeping mechanism with a readable indication of time.
A morning boat timetable with departures at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00, using the landing clock.
Star chart
A drawn record of the stars' positions, used to recognize the sky.
Tripod
A three-legged support that holds an instrument steadily above the ground.
Mounted telescope
A telescope on a stable stand, keeping the view steady.
Arch
A curved masonry span carrying weight around an opening.
Arcade
A covered walkway built around an open masonry span.
Gallery
A sheltered public space displaying pictures for people to see together.
Exhibition catalogue
A portable record of the images displayed in the gallery.
Mosaic pieces
Small pieces of coloured glass prepared to be arranged into an image.
Mosaic
An image assembled from small pieces held in a clay bed.
Ash
The mineral material left after a fire burns its fuel.
Lye
A strong alkali associated with wood ash. It is corrosive and must be handled with care.
Soap
A washing material made from fats or oils and an alkali. It helps remove dirt and grease.
Wash station
A washstand supplied with soap for the people preparing the meal.
Stove
A brick cooking stove with an inset iron pot over its fire.
Cooking pot
A heat-resistant vessel with a broad opening for stirring food as it cooks.
Porridge
Grain cooked into a warm, soft meal.
Fruit compote
Fruit softened by cooking into a spoonable dish.
Feast
A shared meal of bread and fruit, or porridge and fruit compote.
Feast table
The communal tiled table laid with the shared meal. People have pulled up their stools; there is a place for you among them.
Weather book
A bound record of wind and rain observations made over time.
Pond life study
Through the microscope, small green specks drift past a transparent moving organism. This is a recorded observation of pond life, not another instrument.
Wind record
Notes of the windsock’s changing direction and lift. A relative level from the rain collector can complete the weather record.
Filled water jar
The glazed clay jar filled with prepared water. Its broad mouth is still open.
Hearth
A stone-lined place for a small warming fire.
Glass bottle
A clear, narrow-necked glass vessel shaped by blowing air into softened glass.
Cider bottle
The glass bottle filled with cider and closed for carrying.
Dyed thread
Coloured strands ready to be woven into a deliberate pattern.
Weighted seed press
A wooden lever presses seeds beneath a heavy millstone. The draining bed collects the oil squeezed from them.
Waterwheel with jars
Jars fixed around the waterwheel scoop water from the stream and tip it into a raised basin as the current turns the wheel.

Make Stone
Make Brick
Begin beside the river with earth, water, air and fire. Combine them to make useful materials.
We have stone for grinding and bricks for building. Now we need food for the journey.

Make Flatbread
Make Fruit juice
There is a place to cook at the orchard's edge. Prepare bread and juice for the journey.
The flatbread and juice are ready. Next, we need somewhere to sleep.

Build a house
Fit window and sleeping mat
The path reaches a sheltered site without a home. Build a house and fit a window and somewhere to sleep.
The house has a window and a sleeping mat. We can stay here tonight, then follow the path to the brook.

Build a footbridge
Make Handcart
A brook blocks the path. Build a footbridge to cross it and a handcart to move supplies.
The footbridge crosses the brook, and the cart can carry our supplies. Downstream, the miller needs help building a water-powered mill.

Make Grain mill
Make Flour sack
Press seed oil
The moving stream can power a mill. Grind grain for the village and press the garden's oil-bearing seeds for lamp fuel.
The village can now grind grain with water power. Take the sack of flour to the baker.

Bake bread
Pack a picnic basket
The bakehouse beside the mill has a warm place for dough to rise. Bake bread and pack some for the journey.
The bread is baked and packed in the basket. Next, the orchard keeper needs help preserving fruit.

Make Sealed preserves
Pack cider to carry
We have a lot of fruit. Let's preserve it.
The fruit preserves are covered, and the cider is packed to carry.

Fire and glaze the bowl
Make Tiled table
The potter's yard has space for firing and glazing. Finish a bowl that can hold liquids and make a tiled table for meals.
The glazed bowl can hold liquids, and the tiled table is ready for meals. Next, the quarry workers need tools.

Make Pickaxe
Make a wooden chest for tools
At the quarry workshop, make a tool for breaking hard ground and a chest for storing tools.
The pickaxe is ready for breaking hard ground, and the tools can be kept in the chest. The next stop is the river landing.

Build a dock
Make Sailboat
The river is wider here. Build a landing and a sailboat to reach the other bank.
The sailboat is ready to cross the river, and the landing gives it a place to stop.

Build a lighthouse
Make Mooring buoy
Visitors need to find the harbour after dark and secure their boats. Build a light on the headland and prepare a mooring buoy.
The harbour light helps crews find the shore after dark. The mooring buoy gives them a place to secure their boats.

Make Climbing garden
Make Greenhouse
On a later morning, return to the orchard for planting. The preserving work stays in the earlier workspace while you prepare support and shelter for growing plants.
The climbing plants have support, and the tender plants have shelter. The uphill beds still need water.
Make Irrigated garden
The stream is below the growing beds. Use the current to lift water into a raised basin, then bring it to the garden without carrying every bucket uphill.
Water now reaches the garden without being carried uphill in buckets.

Make Festival banner
Make Canopy
Neighbours are coming to the village square for music and a shared meal. Make a banner and a canopy for shade.
The square has a banner and a canopy for shade. Now we can send invitations to our neighbours.
Make charcoal for ink
We stop at the quarry kiln for charcoal. At the landing, we can grind it into ink for our invitations.
The cooled charcoal is ready to carry to the landing. The kiln stays at the quarry.

Make Mailboat
Make Printed invitations
We need to invite our neighbours to the meal and music. Back at the landing, prepare printed invitations and a mailboat to carry them.
The invitations are printed and the mailboat is ready to carry them. Next, we need instruments for the musicians.

Make Flute
Make Drum
Make Bandstand
The following afternoon, the square is ready for music. Make instruments and a raised place for the players.
The flute, drum and bandstand are ready. The musicians can play while we prepare a puppet show for the children.

Make Puppet theatre
Make Picture book
Later, children gather in the square. Prepare a puppet theatre and a picture book for them.
The puppet theatre and picture book are ready for the children. Next, we can examine the small living things in the pond.
Examine pond slide
At the millpond, examine a water sample more closely. A microscope can reveal things too small to see unaided.
We can see tiny living things in the pond sample. Next, we can examine leaves and record the plants beside the river.
Make Illustrated flora
On another orchard morning, visitors want to identify the plants. Make illustrated records they can compare with living examples.
The plant guide contains preserved specimens and drawings. Visitors can compare a plant with its description and picture.
Make Weather record
Back at the headland, boat crews want a record of changing weather. Prepare observations they can compare over time.
The record brings the wind and rain observations together. Boat crews can use it to compare the conditions over time.

Make Smoked fish
Make Pickle jar
At the tidal shore, boats are preparing for a crossing without a cooking hearth. Preserve food that the crews can take with them.
The smoked fish and pickles are packed for the crossing boats. Visitors are arriving at the landing for the meal and music.
Visitors have arrived at the landing for the meal and music.

Make Washstand
Fill and cover the water jar
Our visitors have arrived. Prepare a place to wash and a covered jar of water for them.
The visitors have water and a place to wash. The cooks also need a washing station before they prepare the meal.
Make Wash station
The visiting cooks want to help. Finish the washing station around the corner before they start preparing food.
The cooks have soap and a washstand. We can now help them prepare the meal.

Cook porridge
Cook fruit compote
Lay a feast table
The cooks and guests are here. Prepare porridge and fruit compote, then set the table for a shared meal.
The porridge and fruit compote are ready. Everyone can share the meal at the table.

Make Grain bin
Make Fruit crock
After preparing the meal, put food aside in the village's dry store. Leave grain and preserved fruit for later use.
The grain is in its dry bin, and the dried fruit is in a covered crock for later meals.

Make Floating lantern
Make Watch lamp
At dusk, return to the landing to prepare lights. The evening boats need a visible welcome and the watch needs a lamp.
The night watch has a protected lamp. The floating lantern is ready for the sheltered basin at the landing.
Schedule hourly return boats
The next morning, guests need to know when their boats leave. Use the landing clock to make an hourly departure schedule.
The timetable shows departures at nine, ten and eleven o'clock. Passengers can check when their boat leaves.

Chart the stars
Make Mounted telescope
The following evening, some visitors stay to observe the stars. Return to the headland to make a chart and mount a steady telescope.
The telescope is mounted steadily, and the star chart helps visitors identify what they see.

Make Exhibition catalogue
Make Mosaic
The next day, display the pictures and records in the square. Make a catalogue and a mosaic for the exhibition.
The pictures and mosaic are on display. Visitors can take a catalogue of the exhibition.
Place floating lantern at the gathering landing
It is evening. Put the floating lantern in the sheltered basin at the landing.
The lantern floats in the sheltered basin. The neighbours have a shared table, working equipment and places to meet, learn and make things.
Plants can provide food, fibres, seeds and wood. Growing them supplies materials people can harvest and use.
A new possibility
A wheel can carry a load by rolling or transfer turning motion in a machine. Its shape makes new kinds of transport and work possible.
The waterwheel, gears and grinding stone are connected. Flowing water can now do the repeated work of grinding grain for the village.
Iron can be shaped into strong cutting edges, fasteners and fittings. It adds new possibilities for tools and construction.
The boat can use wind in its sail to move across the water. It gives the neighbours a way to travel between the banks.
The carved block can print the same invitation on many sheets. Several messengers can now invite neighbours to the meal and music.
The microscope reveals details too small for unaided sight. A prepared pond-water sample can now be examined for tiny living things.
Soap helps people wash away dirt and grease. Beside a washstand, it makes everyday washing more useful.
The clock gives a shared, readable time. People can use it to agree on meetings and boat departures.
